subject: Information Theory
title: Braille and Encoding
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Braille and Encoding.

hook.text: Braille uses six raised dots in a 2×3 grid. That's 64 possible patterns—a 6-bit code designed for fingertips.

buildup.text: Louis Braille invented it at age 15 in 1824, adapting a military night-reading system for blind readers.

discovery.text: Each cell encodes one character. Contractions combine cells: 'the' becomes one symbol in Grade 2 Braille.

twist.text: Braille contractions are a form of compression—frequent words get shorter representations, just like Huffman.

climax.text: From Shannon's view, Braille is a channel-matched code: optimized for the bandwidth of human touch.

punchline.text: Six dots. 64 patterns. A code for fingers.

quiz.question: How many possible patterns does a standard Braille cell have?
